explain.say: At around 12 metres a second the turbine reaches its rated, or full, power. In stronger wind the blades pitch to spill the extra, keeping the power flat so nothing is overloaded.

faq.q: What is a cut-in wind speed?
faq.a: It is the lowest wind speed at which a turbine starts making useful electricity, usually around 3 to 4 metres a second, a gentle breeze. Below that, the energy is not worth collecting.
asks: Why don't wind turbines turn in light wind?

faq.a: Rated power is the most a turbine is built to produce, reached at around 11 to 13 metres a second. Above that, the blades are angled to hold the power steady.
asks: What does a wind turbine's megawatt rating mean?

faq.q: Why do wind turbines stop in strong winds?
faq.a: In a gale, around 25 metres a second, the forces on the blades and tower become dangerous. The turbine turns its blades edge-on to the wind and brakes, then restarts when the wind drops.
asks: Why are wind turbines not turning on a windy day?

faq.q: Why does a little more wind make so much more power?
faq.a: The power in wind goes with the speed cubed. Double the wind speed and eight times as much power flows through the blades.
asks: Why is the power curve so steep?

faq.q: Can a turbine catch all the wind's energy?
faq.a: No. If it took all the energy, the air would stop dead behind it and no more could flow through. The most any turbine can capture is about 59 percent, called the Betz limit, and good turbines reach around 45 to 50 percent.

facts: The Betz limit, worked out by Albert Betz in 1919, says no wind turbine can capture more than about 59 percent of the wind's energy.
The power carried by the wind is proportional to the cube of its speed.
